#9135. Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

Photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation. The landscape is immense, the conditions can be demanding, and the opportunities to make a particular image may be limited to a few minutes. Towering icebergs, drifting sea ice, fog, low clouds, and the changing Arctic sky create an environment in which light can completely transform the way a scene is perceived. Yet having spectacular scenery in front of you does not necessarily mean you will come away with a strong photograph. The challenge is to recognize what makes a moment worth capturing, understand how the available light interacts with the landscape, and make the right decisions before that moment disappears.

During a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice. These two subjects offered very different photographic challenges and a particular one-of-a-kind night operation.

Some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag. The moonrise series was one of those projects. Across four days, I followed the changing opportunities to photograph the rising moon among the enormous icebergs of East Greenland. The objective was not simply to record the moon above the horizon, but to find a relationship between the moonlight, the architecture of the icebergs, the sense of exploration, and the surrounding landscape.

The first opportunity to photograph the sequence came around 8 p.m. on day three of our expedition, when the timing and the available light finally began to align. In the Arctic, twilight can retain considerable ambient light even as the moon rises. This transition creates an interesting balance: the landscape may still hold detail, while the moon begins illuminating the ice from a different angle.

A rising moon and a monumental iceberg are impressive subjects individually, but putting them together is not enough. Their positions, relative sizes, illumination, and separation from the background all influence how the image is read. Anticipating these relationships is essential, particularly when the window for making the photograph is short.

Photographing from a Zodiac adds another dimension to the process. Polar bear presence in East Greenland limits our possibility to operate on land during low-light conditions. Unlike working from stable ground, the shooting position is not necessarily fixed, and even small movements can affect the framing, particularly when using a long focal length.

The objective was to find a viewpoint from which the iceberg formations could be separated visually and the rising moon incorporated without losing the sense of scale. Icebergs are difficult subjects to photograph because their dimensions can be hard to communicate.

Focal length plays an important role in communicating scale. A wide-angle lens can emphasize the surrounding environment, while a longer lens can compress the scene and bring distant formations visually closer together.

Exposure requires similar care. A gradually brightening moon against a dark sky can make it difficult to preserve highlights without losing detail in the shadows. Rather than trying to make every part of the photograph equally bright, I aim to retain the texture of the illuminated surfaces while allowing darkness to remain part of the image, preserving my highlight and shadow information.

The Northern Lights create a very different set of challenges. The moon’s position can be anticipated, allowing me to plan around a relatively predictable source of illumination. This is great for subject illumination, though distracting when the moon appears in the frame. The aurora, by contrast, can change rapidly in brightness, shape, color, and movement.

From our main vessel, we navigate through the fjord in search of a good-looking iceberg to frame our shot. We carefully position the ship to achieve the greatest possible stability while maintaining the flexibility to adjust our orientation depending on where the aurora is expected to appear. The moment the Northern Lights emerge, close coordination via VHF radio with the bridge team becomes essential. As we prepare to photograph from the ship’s outer deck, the vessel is brought to a complete standstill, reaching zero speed over ground. This allows us to capture the scene with maximum stability, even using exposures of around half a second, while the iceberg and the dancing aurora create the perfect natural composition.

Aurora photography involves a series of compromises between shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. A longer exposure collects more light, which can help when the display is faint, but it can also blur the finer structures of a rapidly moving aurora. A shorter exposure preserves more detail in the curtains and patterns but requires enough light to produce a usable image. There is no universal exposure for the Northern Lights. The right settings depend on the brightness and speed of the display, the available ambient light, the lens, and the amount of detail I want to retain. I adjust according to the behavior of the sky rather than relying on a fixed recipe, as shown below with this powerful curtain of light.

As the sun began to set, we left the comfort of our main vessel and ventured out aboard our Zodiacs for a reconnaissance ride through the surrounding waters. Our mission was to explore the landscape, identify one or two particularly striking icebergs, and select the perfect setting for what we hoped would become an unforgettable night of aurora photography. Capturing the Northern Lights is as much about patience and preparation as it is about being in the right place at the right time. With exposures ranging from half a second to four, five, or even six seconds, stability becomes essential. Even the slightest movement can compromise an image. Out here, surrounded by the vastness of the polar landscape, finding a way to create a stable photographic platform would be one of the greatest challenges of the night.

Our idea was to return after dark, launching the Zodiacs from the main vessel and navigating through the freezing waters in search of newly formed sea ice near one of the selected icebergs. This young ice, approximately one centimeter thick, offered the possibility of carefully positioning the bow of a Zodiac against its edge, allowing us to wedge ourselves into place and create the stability required for long exposures. Finding a sufficiently wide area of newly formed ice would also give us the freedom to reposition ourselves as the auroras shifted and danced across different parts of the sky. But this was about more than simply finding a stable platform. It was about finding the right perspective, in pitch darkness surrounded by the freezing Greenlandic waters.

When planning an operation like this, I always look for ways to approach an iceberg while maintaining a safe distance and shooting from as low an angle as possible. I want the iceberg to become a powerful element in the composition, rising beneath the aurora and giving the image a strong sense of scale and depth. The newly formed sea ice often adds another dimension to the scene. Its delicate patterns, textures, and natural leading lines can guide the viewer’s eye toward the main subject, transforming an already extraordinary landscape into a compelling photographic composition.

By 11 p.m., it was time. We left the main vessel and began our night mission. Alongside my teammates Signe-Maria and Myriam, I led our group of photographers toward the giant icebergs and the newly formed sea ice. Behind us, the ship’s powerful searchlight illuminated our chosen iceberg, providing a guiding beacon across the darkness as we made our way toward our destination. Once we reached the area, we carefully positioned the Zodiacs against the edge of the newly formed ice. Every movement had to be deliberate. We wanted to achieve the stability needed for photography while maintaining a safe distance from the iceberg and the surrounding ice.

Fortunately, we had prepared for this moment long before leaving the ship. During the day, we had already assembled, adjusted, and practiced our photographic setups, making sure everyone knew exactly what to do. Now, under the darkness of the polar night, there was no time to waste. We secured our tripods against the Zodiac’s pontoon and tilted them forward, carefully adjusting their position to keep every part of the Zodiac out of the frame. One by one, our photographers settled into their compositions, pointing their cameras toward the magnificent icebergs.

Everything was ready. I picked up the radio and called the ship’s bridge team, asking them to switch off all the lights. And suddenly, everything changed. The powerful beam that had guided us across the darkness disappeared. We were now completely immersed in the polar night, resting on the newly formed sea ice, facing a gigantic iceberg beneath an extraordinary celestial spectacle. Above us, twenty billion stars seemed to fill the sky. A half-moon gently illuminated the frozen landscape, revealing the magnificent shapes and textures of the iceberg, while the auroras began dancing overhead, bringing movement and color to an otherwise silent world.

For a moment, everything seemed to stand still. There we were, floating between the ocean and the ice, surrounded by one of the most extraordinary landscapes on Earth. Cameras were clicking, shutters were opening and closing, and each long exposure was capturing a fleeting moment of this ever-changing spectacle. It is difficult to describe the feeling of witnessing such a scene. You can plan every detail, prepare your equipment, study the conditions, and carefully orchestrate the entire operation, but nature always has the final word. And when everything finally comes together, the experience goes far beyond photography. That night, we were fortunate enough to experience something truly exceptional. A moment in which preparation, teamwork, adventure, and nature converged beneath the dancing auroras. The photographs will remain on our SD cards, but the feeling of being there, surrounded by the icebergs, the stars, and the silence of the polar night, will remain with us forever.

There is a tendency to describe photographs of the Arctic as the result of being in the right place at the right time. Luck certainly plays a role. The moon must rise in a favorable position, the weather must allow the landscape to be seen, and the aurora must develop in a way that creates an interesting composition. None of these conditions can be guaranteed. But being present when a spectacle occurs is only part of the process. The photographer must recognize the potential of the scene, decide where to position the camera, choose a focal length, balance the exposure, and determine which elements belong in the frame. Preparation does not control nature; it makes it possible to respond when an opportunity appears.

#9132. Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale. Explore how thoughtful layering brings distant views to life by connecting nearby details with the features that make a location memorable.

Creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another. Foreground details establish scale, middle-ground features connect the viewer to the wider landscape, and distant elements provide context. When these elements complement one another, they give the photograph greater dimension and draw the viewer through the frame.

Getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range. Camera position, focal length, overlapping shapes, and changing light all influence how layers appear and how easily the viewer can distinguish them. This guide explores how to apply these techniques in the field—from recognizing natural layers and arranging them within the frame to avoiding visual clutter.

The foundation of a layered landscape composition is the relationship between its foreground, middle ground, and background. These three zones provide a visual structure that communicates distance and gives the viewer a sense of moving through the scene. The foreground is the area closest to the camera, the middle ground occupies the space between the viewer and the distant scenery, and the background typically contains the farthest elements, such as mountains, hills, or the sky.

Each layer serves a distinct purpose. The foreground anchors the immediate setting and gives the viewer an entry point. The middle ground bridges that starting point to the rest of the landscape, while the background provides context, scale, and a sense of distance. When these elements work together, the photograph feels far more dimensional than a composition built around a single distant subject.

Not every landscape needs three clearly defined layers. A photograph of a mountain reflected in a lake, for example, might rely on two dominant planes, while a forest scene could contain several overlapping layers of trees. The goal is not to force every scene into a rigid formula, but to recognize the distinct planes of distance within it and decide how each contributes to the composition.

Before setting up the camera, take a moment to identify what occupies each part of the view. Look for elements that naturally lead the eye through the frame, as well as areas that might compete for attention. Taking this step helps determine whether the scene already has a strong visual structure or whether changing your position could reveal a more effective arrangement.

A strong foreground gives a landscape photograph an immediate point of entry. Rocks, grasses, wildflowers, fallen trees, shoreline details, and other nearby features establish a sense of place while making the distance feel more pronounced. Rather than simply filling the bottom of the frame, the foreground should serve a clear purpose in the composition.

Look for foreground elements that relate to the larger scene. A line of rocks leading toward a mountain, a patch of wildflowers beneath a distant ridgeline, or a weathered tree framing a valley can connect the viewer to the landscape beyond. These details establish scale and make an expansive scene feel more tangible.

Camera position has a considerable effect on how prominent the foreground becomes. Lowering the camera gives nearby objects greater visual weight, often exaggerating their apparent size relative to the background. This can create a dramatic sense of depth, particularly when using a wide-angle lens. However, getting too close can make a foreground object overwhelm the rest of the photograph. Move the camera forward and backward while checking how much space the foreground occupies and whether it remains connected to the distant view.

Pay attention to the edges of the frame as well. A partially cropped rock, branch, or other object along the border can look accidental if it draws attention without adding to the composition. Sometimes shifting the camera just a few inches is enough to position the foreground more deliberately. If there is no suitable foreground element, resist the urge to include something merely to fill the space. A clean, uncomplicated foreground is often more effective than one that distracts from the landscape.

The middle ground is often the most overlooked part of a landscape composition. Photographers frequently concentrate on finding an interesting foreground and capturing a dramatic background, leaving the space between them without a clear visual role. Yet this middle zone is essential because it bridges near and distant elements, helping the photograph feel cohesive.

Middle-ground subjects can include rolling hills, tree lines, rivers, fields, valleys, waterfalls, or clusters of rocks. These features smooth the transition between planes of distance and can create a natural path through the image. A river winding between a foreground shoreline and distant mountains, for example, gives the viewer a route through the landscape. A series of hills can create successive bands that gradually recede toward the horizon.

Look for shapes and lines that link different parts of the scene. A sloping hillside might echo the angle of a nearby rock formation, while a line of trees could guide attention toward a distant peak. Repeating forms also help unify a composition; a series of ridges or tree-covered slopes creates a visual rhythm that reinforces depth.

If the middle ground feels empty, consider whether changing your position reveals more of the landscape between the foreground and background. Moving laterally along a trail or shoreline can shift the relationship between overlapping features and expose details that were previously hidden. You may also find that a slightly longer focal length brings distant layers together more effectively, especially in landscapes with repeating hills or ridgelines.

The background gives a landscape its broader context, but distant elements can easily lose definition when they blend together. A mountain peak that merges with a similarly toned ridge, for example, may lose its shape and visual impact. Creating separation between background features preserves their individual forms and reinforces the sense of distance.

Light and weather often provide natural separation. Sidelighting reveals the contours of distant mountains, while low-angle sunlight casts alternating bands of brightness and shadow across hillsides. Fog, mist, and atmospheric haze also distinguish successive layers by reducing contrast as the landscape recedes. These conditions produce subtle tonal transitions that make distant features appear farther away.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Camera position matters, too. A slight change in elevation or angle can separate a mountain from the ridge behind it or reveal a gap between two overlapping peaks. Before taking the photograph, examine the outlines of distant features and look for places where they merge. Moving even a short distance can create enough separation to make the shapes easier to read.

Exposure also affects how well those details are retained. Bright skies behind dark mountains often create a wide dynamic range, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Check the histogram and highlight warnings to avoid losing important sky detail. If necessary, use exposure bracketing or a graduated neutral density filter to manage the difference in brightness. Preserving tonal detail across the scene helps maintain the distinction between distant layers.

Overlap is one of the most direct ways to communicate depth in a landscape photograph. When one object partially obscures another, the viewer immediately recognizes that the two elements occupy different planes of distance. A foreground tree overlapping a distant ridge, for example, creates a clear spatial relationship even though the photograph is a two-dimensional image.

Look for natural arrangements where landscape features overlap cleanly. Successive mountain ridges, layers of trees, and rolling hills are particularly useful because they provide repeated shapes at different distances. The viewer can follow these forms as they recede into the background, creating a sense of depth without requiring a prominent foreground subject.

How much elements overlap also matters. If one element completely hides another, the relationship between them becomes less obvious. If the objects barely touch, their outlines can merge into an awkward visual intersection. Small changes in camera position can reveal more of one feature or create a cleaner separation between them.

This is especially important when photographing forests or densely layered landscapes. Branches and tree trunks can easily intersect in ways that make the image feel tangled. Rather than trying to include every interesting tree, look for openings where individual trunks and branches remain distinguishable. A slight shift to the left or right may separate one tree from another and make the overall arrangement easier to read.

Focal length directly influences how distance and scale appear in the finished photograph. Wide-angle lenses are useful when the foreground is an important part of the composition. Their broad field of view captures nearby details alongside distant scenery, while perspective exaggeration between close and far objects emphasizes depth.

When using a wide-angle lens, foreground placement becomes particularly important. An object close to the camera can appear much larger than everything behind it, sometimes dominating the frame. This can be effective when the foreground has a strong shape or texture, but it can also make the composition feel unbalanced. Pay attention to how close you are to the nearest subject and whether its scale supports the relationship between layers.

Telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Rather than emphasizing the distance between foreground and background, longer focal lengths narrow the field of view and make distant features appear closer together. This visual compression can emphasize repeated layers of mountains, hills, trees, or other landscape elements. A scene that looks relatively open through a wide-angle lens may reveal a more graphic arrangement when photographed with a telephoto lens.

Neither approach is inherently better. A wide-angle lens communicates the scale of an expansive landscape, while a telephoto lens isolates a series of distant forms and emphasizes their relationship. If a scene has several interesting layers, try photographing it at different focal lengths before deciding which version best captures the scene.

Light makes layered landscapes more distinctive by revealing shapes, textures, and tonal differences across planes of distance. The same scene may look relatively flat under even midday light but become far more dimensional when low-angle sunlight creates alternating bands of illumination and shadow.

Sidelighting is particularly useful for emphasizing the contours of hills, mountains, and other landforms. As the sun sits low on the horizon, ridges catch the light while valleys remain in shadow. This creates visual separation between successive layers and gives the scene a stronger sense of form. Backlighting can also be effective, especially when photographing trees, grasses, or other translucent elements in the foreground.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Atmospheric conditions provide another way to distinguish distance. Mist and fog soften the contrast of distant hills and mountains, creating a series of progressively lighter layers. After a storm, breaks in clearing clouds often spotlight individual sections of a landscape while leaving others in shadow. These changing conditions produce natural divisions between foreground, middle ground, and background without requiring strong compositional elements in every part of the frame.

When photographing in changing weather, be prepared to work quickly. Use a tripod when shutter speeds are slow, but avoid relying on one fixed composition if the light is moving across the scene. Take multiple exposures as conditions evolve, particularly when sunlight briefly strikes a distant ridge or a break in the clouds reveals a new layer. These short-lived lighting conditions can make a substantial difference to the finished image.

Adding layers can create depth, but it can also introduce too much visual information. A foreground full of rocks, a middle ground crowded with trees, and a background filled with overlapping mountain peaks may leave the viewer unsure where to look. The challenge is deciding which elements contribute to the photograph and which ones make it harder to read.

Start by identifying the primary subject or visual feature. This does not have to be a single object — it might be a mountain range, a winding river, or a series of repeating ridgelines. Once you know what should attract attention, consider whether the other layers support it. A foreground element that pulls the eye away from the main subject may need to be repositioned or excluded from the frame.

Simplifying a composition does not always mean removing entire layers—it often means adjusting how much visual weight each one carries. A smaller foreground can establish context without competing with the background, while an open middle ground gives the viewer’s eye room to travel through the scene. Switching to a longer focal length can also help trim distracting edges or unrelated elements.

Watch for bright highlights, stray branches, and high-contrast objects that pull attention away from the subject. These distractions become more disruptive in a layered composition, where the viewer’s eye is already navigating multiple planes. Scan the entire frame before pressing the shutter—paying close attention to the corners and edges—for anything that interrupts the visual flow. Often, shifting the camera slightly or tightening the crop is enough to clean up the frame.

Even a minor shift in camera position can alter the relationship between every layer in a landscape. Moving forward or backward changes the scale and placement of foreground objects, while stepping laterally can reveal or conceal distant features. Camera height also dictates how much of the ground plane is visible and how smoothly the foreground transitions into the background.

Rather than immediately setting up a tripod at the first scenic overlook, take time to explore the area. Walk along a ridge, follow a shoreline, or look for a slightly elevated vantage point that opens up the landscape. Observe how foreground elements align with distant peaks, trees, or ridges. Often, the strongest composition sits just a few steps away from the obvious viewpoint.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Once you find a promising spot, a tripod helps you fine-tune height and framing deliberately. Lowering the tripod emphasizes nearby textures, while raising it reveals more of the middle ground. If your tripod has an adjustable center column, extend it sparingly as raising the column too high reduces stability, especially in windy conditions.

Perspective control is also worth considering in scenes with strong vertical lines. Tilting the camera upward causes trees, cliffs, or buildings to converge toward the top of the frame. While that converging effect can work creatively, keeping vertical lines straight requires leveling the camera and adjusting your composition by stepping back or switching to a wider lens. What matters most is whether the perspective reinforces how you want the layers to relate.

Building a layered landscape composition becomes much easier when you approach a scene methodically. Start by identifying the anchor of the view—whether that is a distant peak, a line of trees, a winding river, or light sweeping across a valley. From there, work backward toward the camera to see which nearby elements can serve as an entry point without overpowering the main subject.

Once you have identified potential layers, move around to test different arrangements. Look for foreground features that lead naturally into the middle ground, and check how distant shapes overlap. Watch the gaps between objects so unrelated elements do not merge into awkward outlines. If the scene feels overly busy, simplify with a tighter framing or a longer focal length rather than trying to include everything.

Your camera settings should support both the field conditions and the intended depth of the photograph. For a static landscape requiring front-to-back sharpness, a mid-range aperture such as f/8 or f/11 is a reliable starting point. Focus roughly one-third of the way into the scene, then zoom in on your review screen to verify that both the nearest and farthest key elements are sharp. Optimal focus distance depends on focal length, aperture, and proximity to the foreground; if a very close foreground and distant background cannot both be rendered sharply in a single frame, focus stacking is a reliable alternative when the scene is still.

Keep your ISO low when practical, but do not let the pursuit of a noise-free file force an overly slow shutter speed. Wind moving through grasses or foliage often calls for a faster exposure, even if that requires raising your ISO. A tripod eliminates camera shake, but it cannot freeze motion within the landscape itself.

Before leaving a location, photograph the scene using several different focal lengths and compositions. Start with a wider frame that emphasizes the foreground, then try a tighter composition that compresses repeating layers or gives greater weight to the background. I also like revisiting locations under different light and weather, as shifts in atmosphere or time of day can completely transform a scene’s character and yield a more dramatic photograph. Comparing these variations helps reveal which arrangement and conditions best capture the landscape.

Ultimately, layered landscape photography is about building intentional relationships between elements in a scene. Foreground, middle ground, and background offer a reliable structural framework, but their impact depends on how well they connect, overlap, and remain visually distinct. By paying close attention to camera position, focal length, light, and visual balance, you can create landscapes with genuine depth and clarity.

#9130. Kodak SlideTag Is a $35 Blind-Box E Ink Photo Display and AirTag Alternative

Kodak SlideTag Is a $35 Blind-Box E Ink Photo Display and AirTag Alternative

Reto, the company behind the wildly successful Kodak Charmera, has announced its next blind box-style product: the Kodak SlideTag. It’s a small, color E Ink display with AirTag-like capability and a user-replaceable battery.

The SlideTag uses that E Ink display to allow users to upload their own photos into it and display them like single slides from the golden age of film.

“When Kodak introduced Kodachrome in 1935, the slide mount quickly became the classic way people projected and shared their favorite memories. Families gathered around glowing projectors, watching their favorite moments illuminated inside a simple cardboard frame,” Reto says.

“Decades later, the Kodak SlideTag breathes new life into that iconic retro slide frame, bringing a vintage touch to the digital age. Designed as a miniature memory holder, it allows you to digitize your precious moments and easily carry your stories wherever you go.”

The SlideTag measures 39.3(W) x 46(H) x 7.58(D) mm and weighs just 16.6 grams. The central display is 1.54 inches across with a resolution of 240 x 240 pixels. The color E Ink can display up to six colors and because E Ink doesn’t require any power to retain the image, the SlideTag can display a photo and retain other functionality for extended lengths of time without dying.

The “other functionality” that does require battery power is the compatibility with Apple Find My and Google Android Find Hub. The IP54 rated keychain supports Bluetooth 5.4 and has a real-time tracking range of up to 30 meters while also being compatible with both Google and Apple’s tracking networks. The SlideTag can also buzz on command at 75 dB to help locate it.

In addition to supporting photos, the SlideTay also comes with a host of other features such as a custom QR code for displaying social links or digital business cards. It can also display live daily to-do lists, calendars, event countdowns, or personalized name badges. Photos can be set as simple galleries that only change when the button on the back is double pressed or as slideshows that change as often as once per day. All of the features of the SlideTag require connecting to the Kodak Memory Link app.

Reto is offering the Kodak SlideTag in eight standard styles, with one extra secret design style that is substantially rarer than the others: a silver color.

All SlideTags come with a collectible 35mm slide frame that actually fits a real 35mm slide as well as other small collectibles.

The Kodak SlideTag is available starting today for $35 or as a box of eight for $280.

#9129. Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture

In her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm.

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

#9127. The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo

Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.

ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Detail of Carolina Caycedo, "Neodymium Intensive" (2026), colored pencil, aluminum and variegated metal leaf on paper (left); Installation view of "Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star" (2023) at Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots at the Kemper Art Museum

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, as part of the Counterpublic 2026 triennial, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4. The installation, "Fiesta de la Raíces," part of Counterpublic 2026, will be on view at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition at the Kemper was curated by Meredith Malone and "Fiesta de la Raíces" was curated by James McAnally.

#9126. Kodak SlideTag Review: This E-Ink Equipped, AirTag Keychain Rocks

Kodak SlideTag Review: This E-Ink Equipped, AirTag Keychain Rocks

I have near rock-bottom expectations of Reto when it comes to making a good product. In my opinion, it’s a better marketing company than a product manufacturer, and everything it makes is meant to sell quickly and be forgotten, with the Charmera being the most obvious example. But SlideTag is, somehow, not that. Instead, it is an incredibly good product.

The Kodak SlideTag is not only a cute, fun idea, but also legitimately useful and a brilliant way to allow photographers to enjoy their work and keep track of their belongings at the same time.

With the exception of the Snapic A1, Reto tends to make very cheap, eye-catching products that don’t stand the test of time. My Charmera, for example, is already broken despite not being subjected to anything extreme. Chris Niccolls points to the Charmera as the culprit behind the wave of e-waste we’ve seen from copycats the world over. When we heard that Reto had another blind box-style keychain product coming, our immediate reaction was to sigh in dismay.

But to our true shock, the Reto SlideTag is not only really fun and well-priced, but it’s also legitimately an excellent product.

So what exactly is the Kodak SlideTag? A nostalgic toy? A calendar? A to-do list? A gallery? A slideshow? An AirTag? A keychain?

The answer is yes, and even a little bit more.

At first glance, it’s easy to think that this is going to be yet another piece of junk, but as you dig deeper, you start to realize this is actually not only a useful tool, but also a fun one.

So yes, it is a keychain styled after classic Kodak slide film holders. The frames come in a total of nine possible styles (eight standard and one “secret” special one), and these are hidden inside of the socially acceptable gambling mechanic: blind boxes.

Reto is very, very good at marketing, and that much is apparent in the whole blind box unboxing experience. The SlideTag is not the only thing in the box: you also get a really nice pamphlet showing all the possible options, a little cardboard slide holder that actually does fit a 35mm slide in it (and Reto includes a Kodak-branded one as an example), and a few other little bits and bobs that just ooze style.

Opening the box is just as much part of the experience as actually seeing which one of the SlideTags you got. Almost all of the SlideTag designs are great, with the exception of the pink one, which I unfortunately pulled from my first box. I call it “pig skin pink” mostly because the sample photo Reto shows on the “collect them all” chart does, in fact, show a pig on the screen for the pink one. Chris pulled the Kodachrome.

I acquired two more and also got Kodachrome (which I like a lot) as well as the two-tone green-and-white one. Much better.

The tags themselves have a color E Ink screen that can display photos that you upload to it (up to 12 at a time) and can either be programmed to swap images at a given interval or only change them when you want to by double-clicking the button on the back of the SlideTag. Once an image is uploaded and displayed, it doesn’t take any power to keep the image there, so it should (in theory) last for months.

Even when the battery dies, Reto didn’t go the same route it has with its other blind box toys and actually gives you the ability to swap in a new battery. The SlideTag uses a lithium CR2025 battery, which can be replaced easily by unscrewing a panel on the back of the keychain.

Just having a little rotating gallery of your photos attached to your bag was already a good idea, but Reto went further and made the SlideTag compatible with Apple Find My and Android Find Hub. It is, for all intents and purposes, also an AirTag. Brilliant.

Just being a gallery and an AirTag keychain would have been plenty of value, but Reto kept stacking on the capabilities. In order to use any of these features, though, you do need to download the Kodak Memory Link app. Once open, it is super easy to connect SlideTags to it, and the process is quick and smooth.

The interface will show you a variety of options, including the aforementioned gallery and Find My features, but there is a lot more. You can have it display a to-do list, a calendar, and a countdown (like if you need a reminder of a special event like a birthday). If you’re a content creator, you can also have it display a QR code that it will generate based on a link you give it. This is particularly useful if you’re at a gathering or event where people will be asking for your website, portfolio, or Instagram handle. With this, you can just hold out your SlideTag, and they can go right to it. You can even have it act as a name tag, showing your information if you want to attach this to luggage or wear it as simple identification — the choice is yours.

The charming thing is that as much as there are so many other affordable Find My location devices and keychains that you can buy out on the market, this one’s photographically themed, and I just think that’s smart marketing. Because it has so many more capabilities, it’s a bit more expensive than the alternatives. That said, it’s actually a tag you’ll want to show off and not just stuff in a pocket and never look at.

I think if I were going to have a little Find My location device around the house, why wouldn’t I want it to be Kodak-themed and have things like a gallery and slideshows and the other useful things like the QR code?

Reto is a very smart, well-run company. It knows what to make and what will be a hit, but up until now, the most popular products have also been ones that don’t stand the test of time — they lose their luster in as little as a few minutes, honestly. The Charmera is a perfect example of this, and while I enjoyed it for a few minutes, now mine is just a piece of plastic garbage.

The SlideTag is different. The removable and replaceable battery is a lovely change from a built-in battery that will no doubt eventually die, the utility of the Find My compatibility is amazing, and the combination of that actual, real-world useful feature with a color E Ink display to show off your photos is truly fantastic.

The SlideTag is sold in blind boxes and priced at $35 each. You can also buy a set of eight for $280. That’s more expensive than other tracking tag options, but it also does more. It’s up to you if what Reto offers here is worth that $5 to $10 premium. I, for one, think it definitely is.

There is really nothing quite like this… yet. I’m sure that, just like the Charmera, Reto will be quickly knocked off on AliExpress, but for now, it’s truly unique. You can get an E Ink display, and you can get tracking tags, but you can’t get something that’s both.

Apple AirTagBuy new on B&HApple AirTagBuy used on KEH.comGoogle Pixel TagBuy new on B&HGoogle Pixel TagBuy used on KEH.com

If you’re just interested in the tracking feature, the Apple AirTag, Google Pixel Tag, and Xiaomi Tag are all just as capable (or more so, given the network they use to provide specific locations) and are cheaper. They just don’t look nearly as cool dangling off your bag or keys.

Yes. The Kodak SlideTag is not only a cute, fun idea, but also legitimately useful and a brilliant way to allow photographers to enjoy their work and keep track of their belongings at the same time.

#9125. Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections

Works by Jonas Lund presented by OFFICE IMPART at Art Basel Hong Kong 2026 Courtesy of Art Basel

Insta’ gratification is a monthly blog by Aimee Dawson, looking at how the art world and social media collide. Each article tackles a topic around the innovations and challenges that spring up when art enters the digital world.

How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.

The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also showed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

The importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

The latest “Survey of Global Collecting” from Art Basel and UBS also found a growing number of buyers are bypassing dealers and auction houses to purchase directly from artists

#9124. Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M

The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.

Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

#9123. Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award

Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy® → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies nearly free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying nearly free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

Set calendar reminders for Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer travel. Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. Book the morning the window opens to lock in Wanna Get Away fares at the lowest point costs.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Yes. The Companion Pass works on both cash-purchased flights and flights booked with Rapid Rewards points. Your companion pays only taxes — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights — regardless of how you booked the ticket.

Southwest allows you to change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. Log into your Rapid Rewards account on southwest.com and update the companion information in the Companion Pass section. Plan strategically since you only get three changes per year.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.

#9120. Hilma af Klint Is Rolling in Her Grave

The Swedish artist’s painting went under the hammer for an obscene amount of money. Plus: Lowery Stokes Sims reviews Richard Powell’s new book on pigment, Blackness, and paint.

Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims

#9118. Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

#9117. A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao

“I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”

Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

How long have you been working in this space?

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.
