#9116. The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.

After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

#9115. Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#9114. Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

In a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church, a group of women is sewing the legacies of enslaved people into their quilts.

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

“A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez)

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she says. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”

Within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

The exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”

For a more versatile option, there's also the dual-laser-capable Creality Falcon A1 Pro 20W reduced by $264 from $1,099 to $835. See below for all the best Creality laser cutter Black Friday deals live now.

Aimed at beginners and general DIY/light cutting, the Falcon A1 is a 10W blue diode gantry/CoreXY engraver with a 305 × 381mm work area and up to 600 mm/s speed. It comes with helpful features like a built-in camera and auto material detection, while the Class 1 safety enclosure makes it suitable for home use for personalising items like leather accessories, signs, paper and felt crafts and opaque or dark acrylic pieces.

The 10W A1 is generally too slow for high-volume commercial production, but the Pro model steps up to a 20W blue diode laser. #9112. So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

A how-to guide on all things inventory, planning, appraisals, conservation, and more.

Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing important work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

When it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, said, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

Stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”

When I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

An appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish new cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

Choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”

Artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers.

Christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate plan of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”

Foundations also typically own the artist's intellectual property, including copyrights, trademarks, and in some cases, rights of personality. These are also used for public benefit, both to educate the public about the artist's oeuvre and to generate funds to support foundation programs. A governing board, often made up of art professionals and, in some cases, family members, typically guides the foundation’s activities.

Checking an artist’s archive for condition issues is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

Where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” says Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”

Galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking new representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s.

Prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how big a project is involved.”

Placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She says, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached new museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”

Estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works.

A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation says, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest new visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another issue: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?

One recurring issue involves image use and rights, and estates typically turn to licensing agencies for support. For example, Artist’s Rights Society guides clients through obtaining copyright and intellectual property clearance, legal support, and advocacy. Recently, as estates have tried to balance revenue and reputation, and deal with the easy proliferation of web-based images, some have become less concerned with enforcing image rights.

Auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale.

To do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, says, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”

#9111. Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” said the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges said. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

“The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”

Looking ahead, the judges said “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

“This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

“This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”

#9110. The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

This year’s historic actions demonstrated that Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine will not be ignored — and that the power of boycott has never been greater.

This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed, the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself.

Many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

The massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions.

The Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “anywhere or not at all” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

The first of this year’s strikes, on May 8, was built locally in Venice, with Biennalocene, Sale Docks, and other local grassroots unions whose participation provided legal protection for striking art workers. On May 8, 30 of the Biennale’s 100 national pavilions closed partially or fully, and thousands of people marched from Via Garibaldi to the Arsenale, where they were met with police brutality. Many artists in the main exhibition draped or altered their works.

The second strike, on June 12, was national in scale. It was the result of a year of organizing assemblies and actions in about 20 cities all around Italy, with organizations including Mi Riconosci?, Vogliamo Tutt’Altro, Biennalocene, and grassroots unions through the Cultural Strike platform.

The third strike, on 30 October, responded to a call that emerged from outside the art world from the World Federation of Trade Unions and, in Italy, was taken up by militant dockworkers, including the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers, and the grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base. A network of port unions at 113 in 22 countries, including Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, and Morocco, refused to load weapons bound for Israel. This was the biggest ever coordinated action of its kind, and our role was to help build local participation in Venice.

Today, November 20, as this piece is being published, the International Student Strike brought further strike action to Venice, demonstrating the political convergence between students and the Biennale — students in the city are often employed in the cultural sector under precarious conditions.

Our ability to do this grew out of the work we began in 2024, in adherence to the guidelines of the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) and Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS), when our open letter demanding Israel’s exclusion from the Biennale was signed by more than 24,000 cultural workers. That year, the Israel pavilion closed.

Between 2024 and 2026, our campaign connected more substantively with the Italian labor movement. As the June 12 strike articulated, the political atomization of artists is a labor issue, related to the art world’s reliance on precarity, which shifts the risk of political action onto individuals. The Biennale provides no fees or production money to artists, leaving them to fundraise their participation. Those whose work is not sufficiently market-friendly to claw back payment in future sales have to content themselves with being paid in the false currency of prestige.

ANGA refuses the oppressive logic that allows the Biennale to support genocide and profit from precarious labor while claiming to rise above politics. This year, we have made clear that the alliance we have created has the power to disrupt the Biennale’s functioning and change its nature.

Today, the contradictions of the present political order — the indigestible, white-supremacy-coded cocktail of Europe’s simultaneous opposition to Russia and support for Israel; the flailing, ever-dying economy; the oceans of money poured into technologies of death and destruction — explode messily into the supposedly morally hermetic market-world of the Biennale.

The farcical “Visitors’ Lions” are the Biennale’s wager that the walls can always be painted pure white again. But this year’s massive actions have demonstrated that we will not allow Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine to be art-washed and ignored. ANGA’s members and supporters are no less steadfast than we were three years ago, when our campaign first began. It remains obvious and undeniable that Israel, the United States-backed abattoir-state, must not be allowed to bring its logic of butchery to be art-washed into neutral “complexity” at the Biennale. And we are now considerably more organized and better connected to the wider struggle against Zionism.

When we look back to ANGA’s beginnings, in early 2024, we remember a time when the shock of total Zionist impunity was still raw enough to feel unreal. We could not imagine that friends or colleagues could disagree with this basic principle. We were soon disabused, as many cultural workers washed their hands of blood in service of their careers.

But our collective efforts have transformed this anti-political status quo. The new compositions of struggle made possible by the mass revolt against Zionism offer a model for how the art world can reach beyond the isolated precarity of cultural labor into new alliances — with students, with dockworkers. The power of boycott as a tool has never been greater. We continue to remake the Venice Biennale, the modern world exhibition, from Walter Benjamin’s “place of pilgrimage to the commodity fetish” into a site of struggle.

#9108. In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

An intergenerational group of artists confronts technology as both a pathogen and a cure for today’s cultural ailments in the husk of an office at 260 Madison.

A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

“We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”

Rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a new immersive Japanese hentai company through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

Both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a new work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion.

Having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators said they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols.

“He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva said regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very important work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”

Meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the New Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

Yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

“My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.

Tabak was particularly interested in curating works that “blur the line between the hand and technology,” inviting artists who “haven’t had a lot of chances to show in art contexts, whether it’s because they are in the design world or have nine-to-fives,” to participate in the exhibition. She explains that many of them complicate the very notion of technology and its use, citing Brian Oakes’s “Vessel 9” (2025), which gathers 3D-modeled circuit boards into a suspended “techno-Gothic” chandelier, and Ryan Decker’s “The Wavemaker Falters” (2026), which uses a motorized, rudder-like instrument to swoosh water through a raised vessel resembling a spaceship.

“We view technology not as something that has arrived in the 20th century, but something that has made humanity possible,” Matasheva said, expanding on Tabak’s comment. “Language is a technology, a chisel is a technology, everything is a technology.”

While many of the show’s craft-driven works conjure the anthropologist Alfred Gell’s idea that art is a technology that enchants, and in turn, becomes enchanted, others wield technology in the service of care. Kylie Mitchell repurposes a light-seeking solar robot and discarded electronic parts to move a found bird’s nest and egg toward a life-sustaining heat lamp. A few dozen feet away, Gregory Kalliche’s installation “Black-tailed gull nest; Ring-necked Pheasant Nest; Mallard Nest” (2016) suspends an LED light over three metal folding chairs printed with images of bird egg nests. Ben Gould’s “Ark II” (2026), on the other hand, augments a hospital gurney with eight aluminum armatures that hold fresh red roses inside coil-shaped glass vials. Doubling as a literal manifestation of Shakespeare’s “this mortal coil” phrase in Hamlet, the sculpture’s sterile infrastructure butts against the transitory visual comfort proffered by its flowers, mirroring a healthcare ecosystem wherein privatization, optimization, and tech automation have whittled medicine’s promises of care, healing, and empathy into mere aesthetic veneers.

It’s no coincidence that many of the works in 260 Madison position technology as both a pathogen and cure for today’s cultural ailments. In fact, when the real estate developers initially contacted Columbia University’s School of the Arts, it was to invite artists to “activate” a 36,000-square-foot gutted Duane Reade on the building’s ground floor. The developers eventually retracted their offer and moved the exhibition to the 14th floor, citing ongoing construction. Meanwhile, the original plan for 260 Madison to occupy the husk of the Duane Reade will be realized in a different form next month. Now serving as the building’s new temporary lobby, the former pharmacy will play host to a different group exhibition curated independently by Tabak. Opening December 3, HOW I FEEL will feature artists working across sculpture, social architecture, photography, painting, performance, and programming, including Jessica Vaughn, Quay Quinn Wolf, André Magaña, and 260 Madison’s Grayson Cox and Luke Murphy. How the forthcoming Duane Reade show contends with this moment of tech-induced economic entropy, so intense that even an entity as extractive as a real-estate company cannot commit to its own speculations, remains to be seen.

#9107. A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC

Twenty artists and designers across the Americas will be featured in "Malvestir" at MoMA PS1 this spring, probing the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

The exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach new, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways."

"Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary."
