#9096. National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

Edward Hald, The Fireworks Bowl, 1930s. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman © Edward Hald Estate. Photo: NGC

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

“This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

Daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC

The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”

Tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC

The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka says. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”

Installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa

The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”

The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”

Many who buy paintings and sculpture are now starting to invest in contemporary decorative arts

"l can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from Adobe, so I won't".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing. Into the fray, comes a new artist-led app who's main selling points include the fact that it DOESN'T have any generative AI tools.

NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer. After it was announced on Instagram this week, it picked up close to 30,000 users in 48 hours.

Like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant. But it takes a very different approach. It wasn't vibe coded, and it doesn't attempt to replicate the look, feel or functions of any one existing program.

The project's led by Stuart Semple, an artist who previously annoyed Anish Kapoor by creating a very black shade of black.

"With Adobe pushing AI further into its tools, I wanted somewhere people could still practise their craft and make things themselves. No AI doing it for them," he says. "NIVA is very much our own thing that we've all built together.

Having previously made FREETONE, a free alternative to Pantone colours, with Culture Hustle, he started a Kickstarter for a project that was initially called Abode. He raised $240,000 from 3,000 backers, a few hundred of whom have been using the software regularly over a year and a half of beta testing. Around 10 people were involved more heavily in making the software, but Stuart says he largely built it himself "with help from some geeky friends from time to time when I've got stuck."

At some point the name changed, and the project became NIVA. "I can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from the lawyers representing Adobe for legal reasons, so I won't," Stuart comments.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

NIVA has many of the core tools and functionalities of a program like Photoshop. There are brushes, a pen tool with boolean ops, cloning and healing tools, layers, curve adjustments and blend modes, type tools with kerning, layouts and gradients.

But it's lighter, with a more minimalist UI and fewer menus despite providing the ability to draw vectors, manipulate photos and lay out text and pages all in a single app. Users also get a portfolio page, and there's a visual asset library called Storehouse, where you can store, sort, search and share work. Work can be exported in formats including PDF and SVG.

The pricing model is refreshing too. There's no subscription, and NIVA is free to use for an hour a day. You can buy full-day passes for $10 a time, or you can buy permanent access for $100. If you buy a day pass and later go permanent, the price of the day pass will be discounted. This allows a full opportunity to try the software before committing.

The response so far has been more enthusiastic than Stuart ever imagined. "I'm so excited and a bit freaked out", he admits, adding that what he finds most encouraging is that over half of the people who used NIVA in those first 48 hours made something with it within 40 seconds of getting access.

"We're finally at a stage where it's stable enough and good enough to share with the world," he adds. It's only version one, the start of something I hope will be great. I still have loads I want to do with it".

You can use the software online at NIVA.design

#9094. Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

#9093. Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds

Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a new study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

The study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing. Related Articles Recent Key Departures at Phillips Point to a Pivot in Strategy The Year in Gallery Closures: A Collapse or a Transition to a Smarter Market?

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent said they had been explicitly denied promotion.

The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

Class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”

#9092. Conservation of the ‘Sistine Chapel of the Andes’ nears completion

Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas, Bolivia Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia

One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.

The US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.

“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.

The restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.

Working on the church’s new roofs Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia

During the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.

Built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.

There are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.

“It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas says. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.

Restoration underway at Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia

The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas says.

The bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.

To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

Santiago’s 19th-century Church of San Francisco de Borja, known for its stained-glass windows, will resume its community role as a national shrine to Our Lady of Fátima after it was set aflame during nationwide protests in 2020

Newly reopened 18th-century Church of the Transfiguration, topped with 22 domes, is said to have been built without a single nail

A 5.1-magnitude quake on 18 July caused the collapse of the roof and part of the facade of the colonial-era Iglesia Apóstol Santiago, one of the oldest churches in the Peruvian highlands

#9090. How do Artworks Acquire Value? New York Art Dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky Weigh In.

How do artworks acquire value? I discussed this complex question with two New York art dealers during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.David Nolan, whose eponymous gallery has been open since 1987, gave the view of an art world veteran; Anton Svyatsky, who opened Management in 2023, provided a newer perspective.

Along the way, we discussed the role of the collector in sustaining value, the challenges of pricing artworks by emerging artists, the ways in which influence and market value have become decoupled, the casino that is the auction house and the zoo that is the art fair.At our talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Svyatsky insisted that collectors need to see themselves as responsible for an artist’s value, rather than depend on dealers and institutions for that function. This shift in perspective, and a return to collecting artists in depth, may well be the key to ridding the art world of speculators. Nolan recalled the immense changes that took place during the 1980s, and the increasing attention paid to artworks’ financial value.Speaking of casinos, a flask emerged at the mention of the new partnership between Artnet and Kalshi—you can catch that moment and other choice ones in the video of the talk above.

From a puddle of bin juice to a fully mapped criminal network, Rockstar wants Leonida to feel like a world that keeps moving when you're not looking.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

“The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” says Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

“Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he says. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger says, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”

#9088. Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” said Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”

Xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

The German-made HEDDphone D1 is down from £599 to £499.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I test out the very best audiophile wired headphones for a living and out of all of them, the best open-back option is hands down the HEDDphone D1. And even at its original price of £599, it's worth every penny.

But thanks to this early Black Friday headphone deal, the HEDDphone D1 is now down from £599 to £499 over at Peter Tyson.

Open-back headphones are the holy grail for audiophiles craving a spacious soundstage, but they usually offer some unique hurdles to achieve true tonal accuracy. When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I said that the German audio company had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

If you do get the HEDDphone D1 it's worth getting a quality headphone stand too. And you really don't have to spend loads of money to get a good-quality, handsome, wooden stand. For me a good option is the Linkidea wooden stand. Even when it's not discounted, under £30 is a bargain.

Usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

At 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.

This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

#9086. Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward

A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, New York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen. Related Articles Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission Fra Angelico's Restored Fiesole Altarpiece Returns to Its Original Church Home After Blockbuster Museum Show

As ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family says Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

Feigen, one of New York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have said they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

But stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes said there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the issue now.

The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

#9085. Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites

St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv Photo by Wavemeart, via Wikimedia Commons

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

The neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

The bombing of several buildings including in the historic city centre—a World Heritage Site—has been strongly condemned by Unesco

The 11th-century World Heritage Site was damaged by a strike on Tuesday

A monastery in Kyiv was set ablaze by a missile strike in the latest offensive against the country, with residential buildings also targeted

The UN body is monitoring heritage sites by satellite and plans a meeting with Ukrainian museum directors to safeguard collections

#9083. Grand Theft Auto VI ’s Vice City Pays Homage to the Bass, Among More Art Easter Eggs

The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

Rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling. Related Articles Carolina Herrera's Wes Gordon and Oribe's Daniel Kaner on Collecting as a Personal Passion and a Creative Practice Art Advisor Sophia Cohen on How the Next Generation of Collectors Is Approaching the Art Market

Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a new character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.

I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.

Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our plans to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

#9082. Construction underway on Jean Nouvel's landmark opera house in China

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped plan, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included BIG, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

8BitDo’s Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Ultimate 3 and Pro 3 are collectables you’ll actually want to use, and the unboxing alone is a treat.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

The metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

Then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

What's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

The less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

This is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

But I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

Switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

#9080. El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years

King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.

A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime. Related Articles AI Model Reveals New Information About Authorship of 17th-Century El Greco Altarpiece 15th-Century Bellini Altarpiece in Venice to Be Restored While the Public Watches

The restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.

The results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.

Alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.

“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.

The restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.

The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.

El Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.

Rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.

Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.

The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.

The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.

When ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.

Reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”

There’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.

For Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.

The newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

#9079. Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument

The Newspaper Rock petroglyphs are among the archaeological sites within Bears Ears National Monument in Utah Photo: Matthew Dillon, via Flickr

Recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

The decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”

The local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management plan for the new boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he says. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”

Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”

Although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo says that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

“When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”

Opponents of the plan say Nine Mile Canyon, described as “the world’s longest art gallery”, is too narrow and fragile to accommodate the widened road and increased tanker traffic

The governance and size of the monument have been disputed for years, and Utah Republicans are still trying to block president Biden's 2021 expansion of its boundaries

The Bureau of Land Management is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of those responsible

Legislators in the state are planning legal action in order to allow mining in region that contains 100,000 archaeological sites

#9077. SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor plan of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely new”, SSdH said.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, said SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio said.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.
