Unreal Engine and an LED wall enabled a tiny film set to create a vast dystopian world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When your physical set is three walls and a ceiling, whatever’s outside the window has to carry a lot of the film. For SNTIENT 2.0, the Fashion Innovation Agency’s film for London College of Fashion, that view was a bleak, abandoned city, and it lived entirely in Unreal Engine.

The story is a dystopia with a twist, set around the idea that resources have run out, humans have retreated into a simulation, and the robots left behind to look after the physical world have started to find beauty in it. “That gave us our visual starting point. A bleak, oppressive sci-fi environment with the potential for transformation,” says Dickon Knowles, director of content at Dandelion + Burdock. The finished film doesn't explore that transformation as far as originally planned, but the city still set the tone for everything else.

The big draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed. Working in a real-time engine meant the team could play with spaces, lighting, and textures, see the result straight away, and change it on the spot, instead of waiting for a render only to find it was wrong. “It made the whole process much more fluid,” Knowles says.

Other routes were tried first. “We tried a couple of generative approaches to creating the city plate for the wall, but resolutions were an issue and the visual fidelity wasn’t there,” Knowles explains. “Which is why we reverted back to our existing Unreal Engine version.”

Even then, the city needed work. The original environment was foggy and slightly desaturated, and wasn't reading through the camera as intended. Knowles reworked the fog, replacing the general wash through the scene with more detailed VDB fog, while reducing its overall presence and boosting the saturation, particularly in the city windows. The LED wall looked better with richer blacks and more contrast, which the fog had been fighting against. It needed a more vivid backdrop to work on camera.

Most of the city was already built before the shoot, with the team making visual refinements, grading and subtle tweaks on set. It wasn't building a digital world from scratch while the cameras were rolling. The advantage was seeing how those changes looked on the wall and through the camera, and making adjustments without waiting for a new render.

The city also ran on an LED wall as the view from the character’s window, which gave the performer something real to react to rather than a green screen to imagine over.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Cinematographer Ben Saffer, whose company, Supervision VP, handled the virtual production, says the appeal was being able to capture everything together. The virtual and physical lighting could be controlled as one, so the glow on screen matched the light on set. “You’re doing it all in camera and capturing everything together at once, and you’re not having to guess at anything,” he says.

The alternatives were a green screen or a pre-rendered backdrop. Knowles says cost was less of a concern than visual quality, because the city content had already been created for a previous project. “The city lights reflect on the performer’s face and on the surfaces of the props and set,” he says. “There is a level of visual immersion that is hard to capture in a studio without the LED wall to illuminate the space.”

The LED wall wasn't simply providing something pretty to look at outside the window; it was lighting the performer and the physical set at the same time, similar to how Magnopus used Unreal Engine for Fallout. The intention was to keep post-production to a minimum, getting the footage as close to the finished shot as possible during filming.

Unreal also solved a budget problem because the film needed a shutter that rises to reveal the city, but a moving shutter built into the set wasn't realistic on the budget, and adding one in VFX would have meant losing that in-camera moment.

So the LED wall became the shutter, rising to reveal the digital city behind it. For reverse shots, a second wall on wheels could be brought in to act as a fourth wall. Because the content ran in real time, the team could quickly render new assets for those angles, animate them, and get them moving. “It was nice to get that in camera,” Saffer says.

Not everything went virtual, though, as the pod itself was a physical build, because the team wanted it to feel gritty and lived-in, with the LED wall and Unreal handling the distant environment. The AI-generated dream sequence at the start was a separate part of the production, created using generative tools to show the character floating in water before she wakes up.

The film has very few beats: the character wakes, the window opens, she looks out. Saffer says the real challenge was getting a sense of the world and her place in it within two minutes. The team also had to make the most of the tiny space, shooting on an URSA Cine 17K 65 with prototype Atlas Lens Co. anamorphic lenses. The larger sensor meant Saffer could capture more of the set without resorting to an extreme wide-angle lens, which would have distorted the perspective.

There was still room for a bit of old-fashioned experimentation. Towards the end of the film, as the character looks towards the window, Saffer held a plastic Polly Pocket toy in front of the lens and shone his phone torch through it from the side to create an optical effect. He also played around with cling film and other materials in front of the lens.

#9060. “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham

Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Click here to check out our Social Housing Revival series.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”

The issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.

“It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham

#9058. Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress

Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.

“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”

The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” said Zimbalist.

“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.

“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

“‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”

Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”

Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.

As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.

Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.

Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

Digital crafting is in rude health, but an omnipresent enemy is lurking in the wings.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Formnext is the world’s biggest additive manufacturing trade show, gathering the best 3D printer manufacturers, large and small, to show off their latest goods in Germany each year. And this year was a blast.

The event is open to the public, but the true purpose of the show is for businesses, factories and retailers to come and do some shopping. This year the show shrank to three halls from the usual four, with consumer grade 3D printing having a larger presence than ever before.

My maker’s heart sang at all the new desktop 3D printers now available, from some of the best CNC machines to the cutting edge in UV machines, to trusty glitter coated plastic!

But AI had to go and make its presence known! It stamped a huge footprint at the show, and response was predictably mixed.

The shocker this year is the SnowPod, a prosumer desktop metal printer that uses a laser to melt thin layers of steel powder within a chamber of nitrogen. It’s launching soon on Kickstarter with a VIP price starting at $4999. Printing in metal is tricky stuff, with more safety hazards to overcome than FDM or resin. The metal dust is not only flammable, but hazardous to breathe, but SnowX seems to have a handle on safety protocols.

I counted eight completely new tool changers, plus two more that debuted last year at Formnext. Prusa, Bambu, Snapmaker, Elegoo, Creality, and Flashforge now have tool changers from four to nine tools, with Anycubic being the lone single nozzle holdout. Crowdfunding hopefuls Axiloop, Co Print and WonderMaker have entered the chat, with nozzle maker Phaetus tagging along with the new Hydra system. Bambu’s H3C is currently the machine to beat, shipping with 8 normal tools and one bonus 2.85mm tool for printing super soft 75A TPU.

UV printing is gaining momentum as manufacturers figure out how to shrink massive industrial machines into desktop printers that are more affordable for entrepreneurial makers. Being able to 3D print full color resin miniatures is enticing, but I’m worried that newbies will be blindsided by the hidden cost of printhead replacement. These easily cloggable printheads are similar to what you see in a paper ink jet printer, but easily cost $900 to replace. And it’s not a question of if you’ll need to replace it, but when.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Prusa Research's newest innovation wasn’t a 3D printer, but a new way to run one. Prusa Connect Local keeps your printers off the internet without resorting to sneaker net and a USB stick. It’s similar to LAN mode, but runs off a local server so you can coordinate jobs for a whole print farm. The server can be as simple as a Raspberry Pi and your “farm” could be a fleet CORE One or a pair of MK4S. The software is free to download, open source and currently just for Prusa machines. I’m guessing that will change as the tech nerds start tinkering.

AI integration in 3D printing is inevitable, and quite useful in some cases. I don’t mind if my printer is monitoring print fails with a smart camera, or if my 3D scanner uses AI to clean up a model. But things get complicated when AI takes over the creative process of model design. Some say AI modeling is no different than cameras taking the job of painters…but is it? Hi3D and Tripo both had impressive booths to sway users to their side.

Denise is a tech reviewer, content creator, and former newspaper reporter with over 20 years of journalism experience. She's tested well over one hundred 3D printers and lasers for Tom's Hardware, and has traveled the world looking for the best tech to share with her readers. You're most likely to find her at a maker festival with her 3D printed RC Death Racer, The Harley Quinn.

#9056. Yuri Suzuki 3D-prints miniature rollercoaster and Ferris wheel for kinetic Onomatopia exhibition

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated)

Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and shows how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.

On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.

The dioramas – a Ferris wheel, rollercoaster, helter-skelter, dodgems and carousel – resemble some of Suzuki‘s earlier work, such as the interactive Sonic Bloom installation in London.

“The ideas have existed in my sketchbooks for the last couple of years and have gradually developed through a series of my public art projects,” Suzuki told Dezeen.

“I’ve always been interested in expanding the scale of my sound sculptures, imagining how they might eventually become architectural structures or even full-scale amusement park rides.”

The designer 3D-printed the kinetic sculptures, which move and are accompanied by their own soundtracks, from polylactic acid (PLA) plastic.

“The dioramas are mainly made using 3D-printed materials, alongside modified HO-scale miniature structures,” he said.

“I had picked up traditional amusement park components – roller coaster, ferris wheel, helter-skelter, carousel, and dodge cars – to visualise my ideas for sound sculptures and architectural structures that could potentially be realised on a larger scale in the future.”

Suzuki has been drawn to amusement parks all his life, and with Onomatopia he wanted to explore how they could help create a utopian city.

“I’ve been fascinated by theme parks since I was a child, particularly Disneyland, but also the relationship between amusement parks, world expos and urban planning, from Coney Island as explored in Rem Koolhaas’s Delirious New York to the 1889 Paris Exposition,” he explained.

“I had the opportunity to work with Disney Imagineering, who create Disney parks, and I became particularly interested in Walt Disney’s original vision for EPCOT (Experimental Prototype of Community of Tomorrow),” Suzuki continued.

“It imagined an ideal city rather than simply a theme park, and Onomatopia is my own attempt to imagine a utopian city shaped by sound, drawing on my experience creating public installations.”

Suzuki, who is known for his sound design, has previously created pieces such as an acoustic playground in Shanghai and a “trumpet-like” San Francisco art installation.

“For me, theme parks and expos are fascinating because they bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience within an imagined world, almost like an experiment in creating a utopian city,” Suzuki explained.

The designer drew on his experience of working on a large-scale sound design when creating these smaller versions of his sculptures.

“Over the last couple of years I have been involved in some large city development projects, such as creating Metropolis Symphony for One Bangkok and my initial involvement in planning around the V&A East (East Bank) development,” Suzuki said.

“I’ve become increasingly interested in how sound can shape public spaces, and my own idea of utopia is a place where sound contributes to wellbeing and encourages communication between people, beyond the boundaries of language and culture.”

Onomatopia is on show at Osh Gallery, The Old Sorting House, 46 Essex Road, London from 10 November 2026 to 7 January 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#9055. mercedes-benz built this orange, gullwing-doored supercar as an experiment in 1970

the 1970 prototype shows a wankel engine, orange fiberglass body and houndstooth interior as it heads to auction with RM sotheby's.

Mercedes-Benz is preparing to auction its 1970 C 111-II experimental supercar in Paris on February 3rd, 2027, the first time one of its legendary C 111 prototypes will be offered for public sale. The orange, wedge-shaped coupe is expected to fetch more than €25 million through RM Sotheby’s.

When the C 111 debuted in 1969, prospective buyers reportedly sent blank checks to Mercedes-Benz in hopes of securing one. The company kept the cars for its experimental program, and a production version never followed.

Only 17 examples were built across the C 111 generations, with 13 surviving today. The example heading to auction, known internally as Car 33, retains its original four-rotor Wankel engine.

The Mercedes-Benz C 111-II made its debut at the Geneva Motor Show in 1970, six months after the original prototype appeared in Frankfurt. Its sharply sloping nose, broad rear shoulders and gullwing doors gave the two-seater a radically different appearance from Mercedes-Benz’s production cars of the period.

Designers Peter Pfeiffer and Joseph Gallitzendörfer developed the original form under the styling project management of Bruno Sacco. The team used an early computer program called ESEM to calculate structural loads, which accelerated chassis development by approximately six months.

The body was constructed from glass-fiber-reinforced plastic and finished in a metallic orange called Weißherbst, named after a German rosé wine. At just 1.12 meters (44 inches) tall, the C 111-II had the proportions of a racing car, with a complete interior upholstered in grey-and-white houndstooth.

Behind the cockpit, Mercedes-Benz installed a 2.4-liter Wankel engine with four rotating combustion chambers in place of conventional pistons. The experimental unit produced 350 horsepower at 7,700 rpm, delivered through a five-speed manual transmission.

Weighing about 1,240 kilograms (2,734 lbs), the C 111-II could accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 4.8 seconds and reach 300 km/h, or around 186 mph. The prototype’s performance made it among the fastest sports cars of the early 1970s.

Sadly, Mercedes-Benz eventually abandoned the rotary engine as fuel consumption and emissions requirements posed challenges. Plans for production ended in 1971, although the C 111 program continued with later diesel-powered experimental vehicles.

Car 33 joined Mercedes-Benz’s experimental fleet in August 1970 and underwent high-speed testing at the Hockenheimring the following year. Among the program’s stranger experiments was a test by development chief Rudolf Uhlenhaut, who reportedly placed butter in the luggage compartment to see whether it would melt during driving.

After decades in the company’s collection, Car 33 became a permanent fixture at the Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart in 2006. Mercedes-Benz Classic returned the prototype to running condition in 2024, overhauling its original powertrain while preserving the exterior finish and interior patina. It subsequently appeared at Pebble Beach in California.

The car now heads to RM Sotheby’s Paris auction with just 24,766 kilometers (15,389 miles) recorded on its odometer. Proceeds will support the Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0 project, while the company has committed to retaining its remaining C 111 prototypes for at least another 25 years.

Mercedes-Benz introduced the C 111-II at the 1970 Geneva Motor Showthe wedge-shaped coupe was developed as part of Mercedes-Benz’s experimental vehicle program

Artist Petter Faustino reveals the secret of painting a detailed environment.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Hi, my name is Petter Faustino and I spend a lot of time painting digitally. In this workshop, I will show you a few of the ideas I like to remind myself of while I paint. I know variations of these tips have been told many times before, but sometimes you need to hear it in a specific way from a specific person in order for it to stick. I hope it helps you to improve your workflow and results.

Painting landscapes is fun, but they usually contain a lot of stuff to keep track of and it’s easy to lose control over a landscape. There are a lot of rules and principles that build on each other, and being able to recognise and find the weak links in your paintings can save a lot of time. I like to work step by step, and I usually try to focus on a couple of things at a time.

I’ve found that simple shapes quickly turn into complex objects, so I like to figure out the big shapes first before I move on to smaller details. There are of course many ways in which to paint, and sometimes you just need to let loose and paint more chaotically, but for me these tips and tricks still work as an overall guide to maintain structure and readability.

If you need the tools to get started, see our guides of the best drawing tablets and the best laptops for drawing. We also have a guide to choosing the best digital art software.

I usually think of forms in paintings as either lying down or standing: e.g., grass lying on the ground vs stone walls that stand up. It is a simplified way of thinking about angles and light, because the ground plane is often more perpendicular to the sun/main light source, and receives more light. Splitting between horizontals and verticals also informs so much more.

For instance, most things grow on the horizontal plane, verticals often cast shadows and they create overlaps. I find that thinking this way gives me a nice start to a painting, creates a natural balance and simplifies a lot of the difficulties with light and colour

Something about big, bold shadow shapes makes the painting process feel a lot more manageable to me. Usually the shadow will play a major part in establishing form and value, but it really shines as a tool for guiding the eye and framing the composition. Dividing the image in two pushes the areas covered in shadow back and allows me to focus my attention on details in the light

I like to keep things simple, and I usually try to build my images up slowly, bit by bit. I’ll start with two or three different elements, big simple shapes in atmospheric perspective, that I split into horizontals and verticals. Then I split those shapes again into light and dark.

This is usually more than enough for me to keep up with and organise early on. Once I feel like the perspective and values are working, I start adding in details, playing with the surfaces, putting in more stuff.

I’ve done a lot of art studies focusing on limited greyscale palettes (three to five tones). This has helped me a lot in both simplifying images and understanding compositions. I think of values like a chessboard: values have to be different enough so shapes stand apart, and the shapes standing apart are contrasted with shapes blending. You push and pull to amplify and obscure. Exaggerating values and pushing a graphical read helps me to keep it simple and focus on big shapes. It also helps me to control overall readability, and allows me to push storytelling by enhancing focal points

I like to use diagonals in my compositions because they are very effective in guiding the eye. Placing a focal point at the end of a diagonal shape is a very simple and effective way of presenting something. I also very much enjoy slow-rising clouds in the background to indicate some movement, which again adds a bit of life into a painting. Little birds or leaves in the wind are other small details that can make a big difference in giving a painting some life and movement.

I’m very fond of brush marks that amplify the shapes they are describing, even better if the brush marks also help guide the eye. Adding details on a flat surface is hard, but you can usually apply patches of dirt and scratches on nearly anything. If you apply marks that follow the established perspective, you are boosting the volume and structure in your paintings significantly. By using value shifts and clever placement, you can also guide the eye through the planes in your painting as you see fit

When working with value, understanding how to highlight areas with contrast is one side of the coin. The other side is understanding how to add structure and detail in areas with low contrast, outside of your areas of interest. When working on structure and detail, in an area cast in shadow or far away in the distance, I use values that are very similar in tone. I think of these ‘low interest’ areas as having their own very compressed value palette. I find that simplified marks allow the details to still be visible, but because of their compressed value range they don’t conflict with the composition or areas of interest

I think environments are a lot of fun when you can stare at them and imagine yourself or a character moving through them. The longer I am looking at a painting, the more I imagine smells, sounds and music. So because I enjoy this in other people’s work, I try to replicate it in my own. I try to make pathways that follow some sort of plan or logic, I add in multiple pathways that go in different directions, and I try to make long view distances so that people can stay a while and hopefully imagine little adventures while they look.

Overlapping is the environment artist’s best friend. It is as effective in primary school as it is in the world of professional illustration. It creates abundance and space, and it does so fairly cheaply, without all the requirements of other techniques. Paired together with atmospheric perspective, it is incredibly effective, and a lot of fun.

To keep things simple in my head, I try to break objects down into geometric shapes when I am painting. This sometimes leads to the painting actually looking very complicated, which is a nice bonus. The first order is to simplify the overall shapes into mixes of cylinders, pyramids, boxes and spheres. But after this, I like to break down surfaces themselves into triangles and mixes of squares. I like triangles a lot because I think they are very effective at indicating different angles in a plane, and they pair very well together. Layering surfaces in squares makes me feel like I’m making a grid, and while that can be great in certain environments, I often prefer triangles for breaking down more complicated, organic surfaces.

‘Pinched shadows’ is a phrase I use to describe shadow in corners, cracks and other tight spaces light is struggling to reach. It is more commonly referred to as ‘occluded shadows’, but I find that to be a very wide category so I’ve narrowed this down for myself, to specify something that is very handy for definition and structure. Shadows are a sliding scale of less light, but we often think of them as something opposite of light.

‘Occluded shadows’ is often used to describe details in areas cast in shadow, but I apply my pinches in the light areas as well. Corners often need a little punch, particularly if the perspective is not indicating the form on its own. I’ll use a slightly darker tone to pinch out intersections in corners and smaller details.

It was a big revelation to me when I learned how much grey is used in a lot of paintings I thought of as very colourful. Left with a strong impression of the colours that were built up to shine, I didn’t really register all the desaturated colours surrounding them. I find now when using this myself that the palette is a lot easier to control for me as well, because I get a wide spectrum using a small palette. I enjoy splitting things, and I often split my colour palette in two early on, but by blending in grey or applying it directly, I often feel like I have more than enough tones to structure my painting around.

Characters often tell a story simply by existing in a painting, but if you can have them interact with something or someone, they very quickly bring the world in your paintings to life. There have been a lot of jokes made on behalf of the famous stick-man and his adventures through concept art, but I do not think we should cast him aside.

Just because something is simple does not mean it is any less effective, and simply by existing he does bring a certain abstract story with him. He also brings a sense of scale, which is great.

Reference is awesome and you should use it, but when slotting things into a landscape, simply using reference can be a detour through a lot of pain and suffering. I often need to familiarise myself a little with the general structure if I am painting something very new. Say you want to put a giant pit next to the character in your painting, but you are unfamiliar with painting pits.

Painting straight from reference, unless you are very comfortable with perspective and volume, can feel very clunky. Controlling the light and value so that they match the scene you already have can be very difficult. In these cases, I highly recommend painting a couple of quick studies and then coming back to the painting and reference after.

Even if you are specialising in environments, I think you should try to study some anatomy as well. I think the more different stuff you paint, the easier it is to build an overall understanding for forms in general, and there are some unexpected crossovers between anatomy and environments.

Ears, for example, can be a great shape for designing unique canyons or spooky sci-fi worlds. They are relatively unique, however, and unless you have that shape catalogued in the back of your mind from previous studies, you might be missing out on a pretty interesting volume structure.

Starting with a basic shape, add details, separation and shadow.

For a big shape, I prefer the lasso tool initially, but a flat hard-edged brush is nice for touch-ups after the initial fill-in. Sometimes it’s nice to have a rough sketch to base the shape on, but you can also add lines over the shape after it is placed, and let the shape influence and limit the sketch.

Here we separate the verticals from horizontals. You can work dark to light, or light to dark, but the trick is to get a good separation between surfaces. You also have to think big and simple: this isn’t super-strict, particularly if it’s an organic shape. Organise your landscape into these two categories.

To solidify the structure, we indicate a light direction and punch out intersections and corners with pinched shadows. We also introduce diagonal surfaces between the horizontals and verticals. At this point, the structure is starting to take form. Smaller details added will follow the same rules.

GTA 6’s animators say the small stuff, from carrying drinks to chained vaults, was worth months of work to make Leonida feel physical.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's a moment in GTA 6 where Lucia is carrying drinks, her hands are full, and she turns around and bumps a door open with her hip. It's an animation repeated throughout the game, subtle but realistic. I picked up on this in my GTA 6 review when Lucia buys a shake and ice cream and has to nudge the door with her hip to get through.

It’s tiny and incidental. It’s also, according to Rockstar’s animators, the kind of thing that took months to get right. I can see why this, along with other little animation flourishes, such as the way Lucia and Jason pull bag straps over their heads to shoulder a loot sack or how they climb in and out of cars, windows, and straddle bikes – little animation touches that build realism.

Mike Jones, Director of Animation: Gameplay Animation, says the aim from the start was a game that felt “fast and responsive yet maintain a weight which grounds our world in realism”. Red Dead Redemption 2 had a slower heartbeat that suited its setting, he says. “Jason and Lucia’s world demands a faster pacing to interactions and movement.”

That pace comes with detail attached. “We put a huge effort into the details,” Jones says, “which means teams caring about something as mundane as how the players might use a door when carrying drinks.”

The result is Lucia turning her back to push through with her hip while her hands are occupied. “That took months of development,” Jones says, “but it matters.”

Moving around is a big part of that. Jones says traversal is “far more fluid than anything we’ve achieved before”, with vaulting and climbing designed to keep your momentum. There are “countless variations” depending on how you trigger an action, and you can branch out and chain jumps together, with the landing changing too.

Rooftops are where it really pays off. “The amount of visual detail on the roofs of buildings is astounding,” Jones says, “and the traversal allows for some breathtaking foot chases.”

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

It's true, I've spent hours in GTA 6 parkouring around warehouse rooftops looking for entrances and secrets. The animation flows with realism, and Lucia and Jason handle ledges and windows differently. Just brilliant.

Mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, says the physical side of the partnership needed “a lot of thought and iteration”. Players can interact with their partner in “a natural, loving way”, with “a believable progression based on their overall investment in the relationship”.

The animators had to find “a realistic balance between player agency and partner response while keeping things fun, passionate, and rewarding”, Tennant says.

All of that sits on top of the everyday stuff. Tennant says there are “close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities”, plus “hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences”. Keeping them consistent meant working closely with the design team across the whole world.

You’ll never consciously notice most of it. But when a character can’t open a door without bumping a hip, it’s a sign Rockstar wants you to feel the weight of Leonida.

#9052. Chipotle hoodie smuggles burritos past the cinema snack police

American fast-food chain Chipotle has launched a hoodie with a hidden, insulated pocket built for one highly specific purpose.

The novelty streetwear garment was designed to keep burritos both warm and concealed while sneaking them into the cinema for illicit mid-movie snacking.

Accessed via a subtle zip at the top of the hoodie’s front pouch, the pocket can also squeeze in an entire burrito bowl or a set of tacos, Chipotle claims, although the logistics of that might be trickier.

Kirby Ann Connell, the company’s senior director of social and influencers, said the launch was inspired by real stories of people smuggling elaborate Chipotle meals into the cinema.

“Movie nights deserve real, craveable food,” she said. “And since our fans were already sneaking Chipotle to theatres, we figured we’d make it a little easier.”

“Sometimes innovation is as simple as putting a burrito pocket in a hoodie,” she added

The limited-edition Sneak It In hoodie features an oversized fit to conceal any bulky contraband, plus a dedicated napkin pocket for any spills.

It comes in three colourways: Nothing To See Here Black, No Burrito Here Brown and Got the Goods Gray.

Chipotle is the latest brand to create novelty streetwear as a marketing stunt.

Other offerings include KFC’s Pickle Puffer, Lego-shaped Crocs and Aldi’s Potato Jacket.

#9051. angelo renna’s eight principles for welcoming non-human life back into our cities

challenging decades of sanitized, anthropocentric urbanism, angelo renna proposes a shift from development to co-evolution, offering strategies to welcome plants, insects, birds, and wildlife back into everyday city life.

Normally, animals live in parts of our cities that are underused or ignored. They are often an unseen presence, almost like ghosts, as we tend to avoid one another in everyday life. Over the last fifty years, human activities have caused the loss of more than two-thirds of the world’s wildlife population, according to a new report from the World Wildlife Fund, stating that their “findings are clear” and “our relationship with nature is broken”. More and more non-human species are forced to adapt to live in urban environments in order to survive. Cities have become extreme habitats: polluted and noisy, dominated by artificial light and concrete. In these unfamiliar conditions, some species disappear, while others adapt to their new surroundings.

Can we preserve nature by looking forward? What kind of world do we need to build for another kind of world to emerge? How should we balance different, potentially conflicting values, such as nature protection, individual animal welfare and human safety? Here is a set of guidelines on how urban design may harness the power to create an environment for other species to thrive.

Creatures inhabited the land long before we built cities on it. Today, some have adapted to live alongside humans in urban environments. Being more generous with them is the first step towards encouraging more non-human urban life. Wildlife-vehicle collisions, property damage, zoonotic disease transmission and physical attacks to people or their pets have negative consequences for both people and wildlife. To help people recognize the value and benefits of wildlife and better understand animal behavior, it is important to promote specific community management programmes that encourage shared responsibilities amongst citizens.

It’s coexistence or no existence’ – Bertrand Russell

Green infrastructure in cities, including green roofs, wetlands, and tree-lined streets, provides valuable passages, stepping-stones, low-speed areas, and refuges where wildlife can find shelter. Rather than always introducing and controlling vegetation, we should allow these green spaces to emerge naturally from species already growing elsewhere in the city. This would entail not planting anything, perhaps not even adding soil, rather leaving any available spot empty and letting the urban ecosystem colonize it.

Located everywhere in the city, in gutters, roadside and in abandoned areas, plants communities coexist and evolve alongside microorganisms in the soil and air. These communities interact with specific urban conditions, including the heat island effect, fragmented soils and heavy metal pollution. Even the smallest plant can attract other organisms and create a unique ecosystem if left undisturbed during the early stages of the design process.

Research based on fifteen years of data collected in North America and Europe has found strong evidence linking intensive mowing of urban lawns, including parks, roundabouts and roadsides, with reduced plant and invertebrate diversity. Reducing lawn mowing frequency can boost wildlife, increase pollinator populations and encourage more diverse plant communities.

Snags, large felled logs, and big decaying trunks provide food and shelter to more than 40% of wildlife species. They offer important structures for cavity-dependent birds and small mammals, food sources for woodpeckers and other foragers, and gradually release nutrients into the ecosystem through decomposition. Decaying trees can be cut and relocated near parks or green areas, helping sustain new ecosystems.

Fountains and artificial ponds help amphibians, such as frogs and toads, with shelter and breeding grounds. Butterflies get valuable minerals and salts from slightly muddy water, while birds use water for bathing and removing parasites from their feathers.

Insects and small organisms occupy gaps and openings that can become microhabitats. The Écokathedrale of Louis Le Roy in the Netherlands offers an inspiring example. Built from discarded bricks, paving stones and construction materials assembled without mortar, it creates irregular surfaces, cavities and passages where vegetation and animals can establish themselves. What might traditionally be considered construction imperfections becomes an opportunity for ecological occupation.

What might traditionally be considered construction imperfections becomes an opportunity for ecological occupation.

Prefer multispecies communities over monocultures when designing with vegetation. A varied composition of trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants increases ecosystem resilience to pests, diseases and environmental stress. It also creates a wider range of habitats, food sources and shelter, supporting greater biodiversity and stronger ecological relationships. Starting from these assumptions, I believe we should envision the city of the future not merely as an urban development process, but as a process of co-evolution among different species within a shared living habitat. This vision suggests an interspecific space in which different forms of life mutually contribute to the construction of a shared environment. It moves beyond the conventional notion of urban development, embracing a broader approach that integrates non-human species into our urban structures and promotes coexistence between humans and other forms of life.

We should envision the city of the future not merely as an urban development process, but as a process of co-evolution among different species within a shared living habitat.

Vice President Deepa Subramaniam discusses the empowerment of creative choice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Over the years, the definition of the 'creative' has been in flux. No longer comprised of classically trained industry veterans, design has been democratised (for better or for worse, depending on who you ask), and Adobe continues to pioneer this adapting creative sphere.

But what does the creative professional of 2026 look like? And with advancements like Adobe Firefly and the increasing development of AI tools, how does Adobe serve this ever-evolving industry without losing sight of the creatives that supported it from the start?

To understand more, I sat down with Adobe's Vice President, Product Marketing for Creative Professionals, Deepa Subramaniam. Together, we discussed how the brand has grown with its creative users, and how Adobe is innovating for the next generation.

Ultimately, a creative professional is someone whose job it is to be creative – that can be as broad or as narrow a definition as you want. The job of a creative professional has dramatically changed: print to digital, digital to web, web to mobile, and now we are in this moment of things changing with AI. Workflows are changing; the expectations around creative work are changing because of what AI unlocks.

How they express that taste and how they put their creative expression out into the world is changing. They have more options for how they want to create: tools, agentic features, workflows in an app, mixing of modalities and categories. But still, the creative professional is the person with taste, creative vision and creative expression.

It's not our job to tell you how to create – it's our job to support you in how you want to create. It comes down to giving you choice. The anxieties get flared when you feel that there is no choice for you, like you're being led down a particular path rather than choosing that path intentionally for yourself.

Do you want to create in flagship applications that are hyper-specific and fantastic for a particular category of work? Photoshop for imaging, Premiere for video and audio editing, etc., or do you want to create in a more multimodal product like Firefly? Do you want to create with an agent in the sidecar or in the driver's seat?

We're just trying to give you a lot of choice. I find that when you give creatives a choice, they make an informed decision. The anxiety lessens because it's the creative taking the steering wheel and making that choice. We want to give them a menu of options to see what kind of shots they can call.

Acknowledging that it's happening is the first step; then it's about helping to alleviate the pressure from the insatiable need for content. The need to create across different media formats, for different audiences, on different device types – it's challenging to stay on top of that.

But staying on top of that is important and necessary to keep navigating the industry. Acknowledging that is powerful – people look to Adobe to acknowledge and guide the way sometimes. AI does give a few ways for you to stay on top of that pressure for content, but not replace your creativity. It can augment your productivity so you can stay on top of all that growing expectation.

I wish I had a crystal ball. We're seeing an increasing need to touch every part of the creative lifecycle. You're ideating, you're creating, you're doing the post-production, you're scaling – that's only going to continue.

There is a move to creative professionals having a speciality, but also embracing being a generalist too. Like graphic designers being social media whizzes or video editors also being able to do sound and colour. There's still a need to be a specialist, but augmented with generalist capabilities in other mediums and categories. That's why we continue to focus on making our applications interconnected and multimodal because that pressure isn't going to go away.

In my mind, when I hear "creative professional," that's distinct from content creator or influencer – but maybe they're two sides of the same coin.

It's about creative vision. The role of a creative professional is changing rapidly from repetitive atomic tasks, allowing them to focus on higher-level creative thinking. Some see that as a blessing and a boon. Others see that as a pretty disruptive change to how they operate. Everyone's on their own journey of acknowledging and accepting that change. A creative professional's vision and direction are becoming much more important.

Oh yeah, definitely. I've talked to people who were staunchly like, "I have my creative process. Why should I change it? It's been my process for two decades." I absolutely meet people who are staunchly not interested in folding AI into their workflow. And when I've talked to them sometime down the road, often they have adopted some form of AI into their craft. Maybe it's subtle, maybe it's pointed, but I think that just speaks to the fact that everyone's on their own personal journey of evolving how they create.

At the same time, this next generation of creatives is entering the industry only knowing AI. There are creatives who learned and honed their craft well before AI models became a thing, and there are creatives right now who are learning their creative expression in real time alongside it. It's wild.

Because it can, when wielded appropriately, be a time saver. It's not meant to replace your creativity. It's meant to enhance your creativity. So you can be creative and get stuff done faster, and be more creative. I really believe that is where AI is valuable.

Whether it's creative craft or software development, AI can take the un-fun parts of your job off your plate to prioritise the fun parts of your job. That's the journey we've been on with integrating AI thoughtfully into our portfolio, and people's usage and reception of it seems to prove that we're onto something.

#9049. Harvard GSD students propose alternatives to Trump's arch

Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation

Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

The students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, worked with Washington DC non profit organisation The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) on the designs. The aim was to engage the public in the design process, as the team views the government did not properly open the arch up for review.

“By recognising Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” said Dvorak and Geitner.

The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum.

“As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum’s course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation,” they said.

“The current administration’s assertion of authority over national memory presented an opportunity to put these convictions into practice.”

The first proposal treats Memorial Circle as “a void along the historic axis between Washington and Arlington”. The designers chose to fill the central roundabout circle, currently covered by grass, with a low-lying pool of water.

A natural stone perimeter surrounds the pool and is inscribed with words of “belonging and unity”.

It’s design is “restrained” according to the team, and primarily meant to be viewed from a vehicle while passing through the traffic circle.

The second proposal does away with the traffic circle entirely and instead inserts a straight thoroughfare to Arlington Memorial Bridge.

Two circular fountains would be located on either side of the road. Additionally, a large pool of water, mirroring the perimeter of the former traffic circle, would fill up the site during commemorative events when the bridge is closed.

It draws upon previous historical proposals for Memorial Circle and seeks to pay homage to the precedent of the site.

“[The fountain] geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity,” said the designers.

“In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”

Trump’s proposed arch was announced late last year with renderings by US studio Harrison Design. It features gilded statues and a neoclassical design and has been dubbed the “Arc de Trump” – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

Construction on the arch was set to begin in September with the government barreling ahead, but it was halted in early November by Judge Tanya S Chutkan.

Trump has claimed the arch will serve as a “military complex” with snipers in an attempt to use national security as a pretext for construction.

Many take issue with the arch blocking views to adjacent Arlington Cemetery, including members of the Kennedy family, who filed a lawsuit to block construction, claiming that the arch would cast shadows over the grave of president John F Kennedy.

The US Commission of Fine Arts (CFA), which reviews projects in the capital city, approved the project in May.

The proposals also follow recent efforts by the legislature to change Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of proposed projects on historic properties.

Earlier in November, protesters gathered in Washington DC in opposition of the administration’s proposed rewrite of these protections. They are couched within the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill recently introduced to Congress.

#9048. Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

“How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”

“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

“I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.

“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”

“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”

“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project

“I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me.”

“I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

“That has been super important for me,” she said. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she said, before pausing.

“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”

So that means you take risks all the time. It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”

Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.

“So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”

Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she said.

“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”

AI tools promise to conjure whole worlds from a prompt. Three weeks in Rockstar’s Leonida showed me what thousands of human decisions really look like.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every week, another AI tool promises to conjure images, environments and characters from a few lines of text. Autodesk and Adobe are among those promising to make creating worlds and bringing ideas to life easier, often with little more than a prompt. Then I spent three weeks playing GTA 6, and it reminded me why I still find artists and designers so bloody impressive.

I've spent weeks exploring Rockstar's Leonida, and while GTA 6 is graphically stunning, it's the little things I keep coming back to. The shopfront branding, flyers that lead you to new characters, comic books on shelves, graffiti and fake adverts. Even Vice City's layout has a personality: all spaghetti junctions, back alleys and beachfront hotels, a world away from the calmer, goofier northern islands.

Rockstar has said it designs buildings by imagining who would live in them and how they'd spend their days. "For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about," says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development, in my interview with the studio. I love that approach. You aren't just making a building look convincing; you're thinking about the person who might have put that sofa there, chosen that colour or let the garden get overgrown.

The same thought goes into the animation, to the extent that Rockstar spent months perfecting how Lucia opens a door with her hip. I properly laughed out loud when a very large resident giggled, stumbled and tipped over a railing into a river. In one bar, a drunk woman trails Jason around, being annoying in exactly the way drunk people are. There's a sequence where you drunkenly try to find your hotel room, and it's the kind of disorientation many of us have felt, both with alcohol and with modern architecture where every corridor looks the same. Out in the woods, two deer nuzzle each other. These little moments don't advance the plot, but they're the sort of thing that makes me want to keep exploring.

The weather is another thing I've found myself stopping to look at, from morning sun cutting through mist over wildflower meadows to storm clouds swallowing the skyline. Rain changes what you can see and hear, and flying a plane through a storm is shaky, stubborn and hard. In a nightclub, smoke and reflected light leave you disoriented, just as they should. In fact, Rockstar has spent years hiding GTA 6's environmental storytelling in details you might never notice. There's an awful lot of work behind getting these moments right, and you can feel it when you're playing.

I've also been surprised by how much I care about Jason and Lucia, and how much of that comes down to the game's art, design and animation. I caught myself shooting enemies in the arms and legs instead of finishing them off because I wanted Lucia to think well of Jason, and because it gets too grim to kill people in a game that looks this realistic. It's an odd thing to admit about GTA, but I started feeling uncomfortable with some of the violence. The writing, animation, and character design had me invested in two people who don't exist in a world built in polygons.

There's a lot of noise about AI generating images, making environments and producing assets faster, and I can see the appeal, but creativity goes well beyond making something that looks good. It's the decisions about what goes into a scene, what gets left out, how a character reacts, when a joke lands and how some seemingly insignificant detail can make someone feel something. You don't necessarily notice any of this when it's done well, which is probably why it's so easy to overlook.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

I'm not anti-technology, and artists have always grabbed new tools. I'm sure AI will find its place, especially in taking the drudgery out of production, but there's a difference between helping an artist work and replacing the decisions that make their work interesting. The latest GDC industry research is interesting reading: 55% of surveyed game industry professionals believe generative AI is having a negative impact on the games industry, while 40% say they use it in their jobs. There's clearly an appetite for practical applications, but that doesn't mean people want AI making their creative decisions.

Leonida is full of thousands of small human choices, from subtle animated gestures to authentically made magazines, fictional advertising and modern art sculptures. I've spent weeks wandering around this place, and I'm still finding things to look at. That's a remarkable achievement, and one that makes me appreciate the people behind it all the more. After all the talk of AI being able to generate anything, I still think the most impressive thing is what happens when thousands of people put their imagination, experience and judgement into making something together.

#9046. 976 triangular modules compose star-patterned timber canopy in switzerland

edyta augustynowicz and summum engineering construct stellar pavilion, a 19.8-by-19.8-meter folded timber canopy built from nearly 3,000 straight cnc-cut beams arranged into 976 triangular modules atop four branching columns.

Edyta A edited by christina vergopoulou November 21, 2026 3 min

Installed on the village square of Stein, Switzerland, the Stellar Pavilion is a 19.8-by-19.8-meter timber canopy designed by Edyta Augustynowicz in collaboration with Rotterdam-based structural engineering studio Summum Engineering and built by general contractor ERNE AG Holzbau. Positioned between the local school, town hall, and Saalbau event hall, the open-sided pavilion defines the public plaza and spans 11.3 meters between four tree-like timber columns to leave the central gathering area unobstructed. Topped by a translucent Polyned membrane that filters daylight, the folded timber lattice draws on two historical references: the neo-Gothic stellar vaults of Basel’s 1912 Heiliggeistkirche and Norwegian-American engineer Kolbjørn Saether’s 1961 research on compression-loaded structural membranes.

Augustynowicz and Summum Engineering unified both concepts in a parametric model where the roof surface rises continuously from the four supports along principal stress lines. The designer used alternating high and low radial lines to fold the canopy, stiffening the shell while channeling rainwater into the funnel-shaped columns for drainage. To rationalize fabrication, the curved lattice is composed of nearly 3,000 straight DUO timber members organized into 976 triangular modules, each combining two diagonal elements and one radial compression member. Arranged in a rotationally symmetric layout in which each module type repeats between 8 and 48 times, the straight beams were CNC-cut while the four branching columns were robotically milled. Carpenters pre-assembled the beams into triangles without custom jigs, combined them into wing-like segments in the workshop, and craned the sections into place on site, closing minor tolerances by hand using the natural flexibility of the wood.

the branching timber columns span 11.3 meters, leaving an open space for activities underneaththe roof stands between the kindergarten and public school, giving kids a place to play and interact

design team: Harmen Westra, Quim Escoda Llorens

subcontractors & suppliers: Timber Structure 3.0 (TS3), Hübscher

location: Stein, Canton of Aargau, Switzerland
